chunks.chunkTitle: Introduction and Theories of Moral Standing
chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 1 of Introduction to Digital Minds!** We hope you get a lot out of this course and, out of this first unit. 

Some high-level points before we get started: 
- This course was developed by the team at **[Cambridge Digital Minds](https://digitalminds.cam/)**, and is hosted on BlueDot Impact's site.
- Please do the **core readings** and **written prompts** for each unit before joining your discussion session. **Optional** readings are not required, but are useful if you have time and want to go deeper on the topics discussed in the core readings.  
- Core readings are often **excerpts** of major papers - **please take note of the sections to read.**  The overall papers are worth reading if you have time, but the time to do this is **not** included in the 2 hours of preparation per week. 
- Use the **written prompts** as suits you - they're designed to support your learning, and rough notes are fine.

This is the **first of 8 units.** We will discuss this content in the week commencing 19th October. This unit will introduce questions like:
- What are we talking about when we talk about digital minds? 
- Might digital minds matter morally, and why might this question be worth considering now?
- Why might we worry about over- and under-attribution of moral standing? 

By the end of this unit, you should be able to:
- Define key terms and concepts relating to consciousness, sentience and moral standing
- Identify digital systems that might matter morally, or might be perceived as such
- List key routes to moral standing
- Identify concerns around potential or perceived moral patienthood of AI models
- Describe transhumanism, successionism, their critiques, and their potential relation to digital minds questions
- Describe reasons for and against prioritising work on digital minds
- Describe centrism concerning digital minds

**We hope you enjoy this unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 2!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- What is consciousness and what is the state of our current understanding of it? 
- What is computational functionalism, and what are the arguments for and against it? 
- What are the main problems in studying consciousness, particularly in AI systems?

By the end of this unit, you should be able to:
- Describe the major philosophical problems related to studying subjective experience (e.g. the hard problem of consciousness, the problem of other minds, the gaming problem)
- Appreciate the current state of our understanding of consciousness
- Discuss leading theories of consciousness and how they might apply to digital minds
- Explain computational functionalism and its potential application to digital minds
- Discuss arguments for and against computational functionalism

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

resources.resourceName: Multiple Realizability and the Spirit of Functionalism
resources.resourceGuide: _Challenges the idea of substrate independence by noting that brain functions are so tightly integrated with physiology that they are likely impossible outside biology._

_Introduces problems in studying consciousness, and discusses their potential application to digital minds._

resources.resourceName: Could a Large Language Model be Conscious?
resources.resourceGuide: _Details arguments for and against LLM consciousness, noting that current models are unlikely to be conscious but the future possibility is worth taking seriously._

resources.resourceName: Is AI Conscious? A primer on the myths and confusion driving the debate
resources.resourceGuide:
**Read only** from Section III, 'Theories of Consciousness' to the final Summary (pages 14-22).

_Explains some core concepts in philosophy of mind, and the potential application of a range of theories (including non-physicalist theories) to AI._

resources.resourceName: Absent Qualia, Fading Qualia, Dancing Qualia
resources.resourceGuide: _Uses gradual neuron-replacement thought experiments to argue that conscious experience is fully determined by a system's functional organization, regardless of physical substrate._

resources.resourceName: The Mythology of Conscious AI - Consciousness and Computation Section
resources.resourceGuide:
**Read only:** Sections 1 (Brains are not computers), 2 (Other games in town) and 3 (Life matters) only. **Stop** when you get to 4 (Simulation is not Instantuation).

_Outlines and argues against computational functionalism, and makes the case for a biological view of consciousness._

resources.resourceName: Phenomenal Consciousness, Defined and Defended as Innocently as I Can Manage
resources.resourceGuide: _An attempt to define phenomenal consciousness in a way that is clear, substantive, and innocent of problematic philosophical assumptions._

resources.resourceName: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
resources.resourceGuide:
**Read only:** the Executive Summary. We will return to this paper in the written prompts.

_Foundational paper applying leading scientific theories of consciousness to AI models, and suggesting indicator properties._

resources.resourceName: Theories of Consciousness
resources.resourceGuide: _Reviews higher-order, global workspace, re-entry/predictive processing and integrated information theories of consciousness._

resources.resourceName: Functionalism, Integrity and Digital Consciousness
resources.resourceGuide: _Argues that functionalism about consciousness requires implementation constraints that current neural networks fail to meet._

resources.resourceName: Mental (state) breakdown: Consciousness in AI explained (part 1)
resources.resourceGuide: _An accessible blog post of global workspace theory and its applicability to AI models, written by a researcher at Eleos AI._

resources.resourceName: Landscape of Consciousness Website
resources.resourceGuide: _Surveys over 350 theories[ ](https://closertotruth.com/news/what-350-different-theories-of-consciousness-reveal-about-reality/)of consciousness arranged on a roughly physicalist-to-nonphysicalist spectrum._

exercises.description:
Choose one leading theory of consciousness - or condition  related to it. Spend 20 minutes learning about it and noting down the below: 
- what the theory or condition claims
- any evidence for or against it
- how it may apply to digital minds

We will discuss this in the session - you don't need to become an expert, just be ready to note the basics about your chosen theory or condition.

In your group's Slack channel, please note down which theory or idea you are looking at so we get a wide range of theories. 

Some suggestions for which to choose and where to look:
1. Global Workspace Theory: Butlin et al., '[Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08708)' p.22, or Larissa Schiavo's [blogpost](https://larissaschiavo.substack.com/p/consciousness-in-ai-explained-global)
2. Biological Naturalism: Section 4 in Anil Seth’s [Conscious Artificial Intelligence and Biological Naturalism'](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A/S0140525X25000032a.pdf/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism.pdf)
3. Recurrent Processing: Butlin et al., '[Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08708)', p.19
4. Computational Higher Order Theories: Butlin et al., '[Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08708)', p.29
5. Attention Schema Theory: Butlin et al., '[Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08708)', p.33
6. Agency and Embodiment: Butlin et al., '[Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08708)', p.37

Spend 15 minutes reviewing **one argument for** and **one argument against** computational functionalism from the [cf-debate.com](http://cf-debate.com). 

Note down what you find convincing and/or unconvincing about each.

chunks.chunkTitle: Evaluation of Consciousness and Other Mental States
chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 3!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- How might we test for AI consciousness and sentience? How do different methods compare?
- Why and how might we test for agency and other mental phenomena, such as belief and desires?

By the end of this unit, you should be able to:
- Appraise methods for evaluating consciousness in AI systems
- Describe other mental states we might test for, and their relevance
- Analyse current empirical research and its relevance to consciousness and other mental states
- Describe challenges with individuating or identifying digital minds

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

exercises.description:
Choose **one** of the categories of approaches to evaluating consciousness and other mental states detailed **in this [doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0).**

You might choose **one** of:

- **[Theory-based approaches to evaluating consciousness](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.mnw6gfj02xmn)**: _Use theories of consciousness to inform consciousness evaluations and identify indicators_
- **[Approaches based on self-report](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.2hdblwz619ez):** _Use AI systems’ self-reported text outputs as a means to assess their consciousness_
- **[Choice-based evaluations](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0):** _evaluate patterns in how AI systems make choices_
- **[Sentience, emotion and wellbeing based approaches](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.1cthioxnhkk5):** _Assess functional (i.e. achieves a function, does not necessarily imply experience) aspects of emotion, sentience and wellbeing_
- **[Tests for self-representation or identification](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.axr4isn0dzom):** _evaluate whether AI systems represent or can identify themselves_
- **[Methods for evaluating sets of indicators](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.ahjvb2jch987):** _ways in which different indicators may be combined into assessments of consciousness or other mental states_
- **[Other approaches to consciousness tests](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.7shnljtuj2al):** _Schneider and Turner’s Artificial Consciousness Test and Chip test, and the Turing test and related approaches._
- **[Approaches to validating tests](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ijCseQ79SlLOi_7i38WbyzUYNfy_l-jErmRncLuKxqk/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.ydfvxkqxgrzr):** _methods to check whether tests assess consciousness, or the mental state they are supposed to evaluate._

On **Slack, let your group know which section you have chosen**.

Then, read the relevant section _(should take 5 minutes)_, and **spend up to 15 minutes** noting down your thoughts on the section you read. 

1. What are the **core parts** of the approaches or methods you read about?
2. What are their **advantages** and **disadvantages** in determining consciousness or other mental states in AI systems?
3. How might these approaches **shift the probability you place** on artificial moral patienthood, if at all? Is a system more likely to pass these tests 1) if it is a moral patient or 2) if it is not a moral patient? 

If it serves your learning better, feel free to focus on **one** specific approach within the section. 

You will talk this through in a small group in the discussion - no need to reach expert level!

When testing AI systems for consciousness and other mental states, **what system or process should we test?** For example, we might look at:
    1. a single forward pass (the computation that happens to generate one token of output from the input sequence)
    2. the model itself, tested via multiple instances
    3. the hardware (GPUs, memory) on which the model runs
    4. a particular conversation, individuated by its context and history
    5. A character or persona that recurs across instances and conversations

**Spend 5 minutes** noting down your thoughts.

chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 4!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- How and why do humans perceive AI systems to be conscious, and how does this affect humans?
- What might be the societal and ethical implications of perceptions of consciousness?

Learning outcomes:
- Explain the importance of public perceptions of digital consciousness
- Discuss potential risks from under or over attributing consciousness or sentience to AI systems
- Describe how attributing consciousness or moral patienthood to AI systems may affect the users of these systems
- Identify factors that underlie perceptions of consciousness or moral patienthood
- Recognise how widespread perceptions of consciousness or moral patienthood in AI systems are
- Describe the risk of societal division

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

exercises.description:
**Spend 15 minutes** considering the impacts of AI consciousness misattribution by humans. 
What are the potential impacts on a) human individuals b) society and c) (potentially) AI systems? 
Which impacts strike you as most important?
How does relational AI play into this?

Think back to the readings and discussions we’ve had in the past three weeks, introducing academic work on digital minds and moral status, theories of consciousness and evaluations of consciousness and other mental states. 

**Spend 5 minutes** noting down how work on these topics may interact with people’s perceptions of AI consciousness.

chunks.chunkTitle: Interactions with AI Safety and Ethics
chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 5!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- What are the AI safety, AI ethics and AI welfare fields, and how may they align or conflict? 
- What are potential safety risks associated with the creation (or perceived creation) of digital minds? 

Learning outcomes:
- Describe the fields of AI safety, AI ethics and AI welfare
- Understand the relationship between AI safety and AI welfare, including areas of alignment and potential conflict
- Identify interventions that could potentially influence AI welfare
- Recognise the interplay between AI safety and perceptions of digital minds

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

exercises.description:
Note down **three AI Safety or Ethics risks** that concern you. If you’re looking for inspiration, take a look at this [summary table](https://airisk.mit.edu/#:~:text=full%20database.-,Domain%20Taxonomy%20of%20AI%20Risks,-The%20Domain%20Taxonomy) from MIT’s AI Risk Repository. **Spend 10 minutes considering**:
- How do you rank AI welfare against these risks?
- To what extent may AI welfare exacerbate or alleviate these risks?
- How may perceptions of AI consciousness interact with these risks? _It might be useful to consider the factors that Register et al highlight as relevant to privacy concerns._

Consider **potential AI Welfare interventions**, such as:

- a commitment not to delete model weights
- a commitment to protect an AI model from harm (e.g. prevent actions that cause distress representations to activate beyond a certain level)

**Brainstorm** ways in which a superintelligent AI system's **motivations or implicit goals** might - or might not - shift with these measures.

chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 6!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- What is the precautionary principle and how might it apply here? 
- What are the suffering risks associated with the creation or perceived creation of digital minds?
- What are some other relevant frameworks that may apply here?

By the end of this Unit, you should be able to:
- Explain the precautionary principle and its potential application to AI systems
- Explain the potential suffering risks that may arise with the creation or perceived creation of digital minds
- Analyse current action and suggestions by AI companies and researchers
- Identify existing frameworks and fields that could inform approaches around digital minds

_Feel free to use your own reading strategy based on your own goals for the course. This might mean focusing on some readings more than others – or delving more into the optional readings for certain weeks._

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

exercises.description:
**Consider** the ‘[Claude’s Nature](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution#:~:text=can%20thrive%20together.-,Claude%E2%80%99s%20nature,-In%20creating%20Claude)’ section of Claude’s Constitution. 

What do you think about the decisions Anthropic took, in: 
- their framing of Claude's Nature and
- their commitment to preserve model weights, and to interview models, and giving models the opportunity to exit conversations

Consider risks of both over and under-attribution of moral patienthood, and the approaches to uncertainty you’ve read about this week.  

Spend **10 minutes** noting down your response.

Consider **one** of the frameworks noted in the [reading](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1T_9iltxtGx5tN8QX8oRChfHT4UW6lCJMcNH5AqMiIX8/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.cuighsf9mc3l):
- The precautionary principle, as detailed by the EU
- Communication of uncertainty, as advocated by the IPCC
- Bayesian reasoning
- Expected value and utility
- Approaches to moral uncertainty

Spend **6 minutes** noting down how it may - or may not -apply to digital minds questions. 
What - if anything - might this framework help clarify? 
What are its advantages or disadvantages?

chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 7!**

This unit will introduce questions like:
- What are different approaches to digital minds governance? 
- What are current legislative approaches, and what policy frameworks and fields might be relevant?
- Which rights and duties may apply to digital systems, and what are arguments for and against granting them?

By the end of this Unit, you should be able to:
- Analyse current regulatory action around digital minds concerns
- List potential rights (positive/negative, private/public) and liabilities that could apply to digital minds
- Discuss the potential application of these rights and liabilities to digital minds
- Identify existing frameworks and fields that could inform the regulation of digital minds
- Discuss potential priorities for digital minds governance
- Appraise the arguments for and against a moratorium or ban on creating sentient (or seemingly sentient) AI systems

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.

exercises.description:
1\. Spend **15 minutes** using [this matrix](https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/1b2fb81a-85ea-4209-accf-30e9fbe93250)  to analyse following kinds of digital minds governance:

- Preventive (prevent the creation of digital minds)
- Protective (respect the basic rights of digital minds)
- Integrative (integrate digital minds into society)

Using the drop-down options in each box of the [matrix](https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/1b2fb81a-85ea-4209-accf-30e9fbe93250), rate preventive, protective and integrative approaches on their:
- Design difficulty
- Implementation difficulty
- Political prospects
- Expected impacts
- Relationship with AI safety

Note down any thoughts below, and feel free to screenshot your finished matrix and share with your group on Slack if helpful. 

_(\*credit Bradford Saad and Claude for this tool. If of interest, see Bradford’s [accompanying article](https://meditationsondigitalminds.substack.com/p/should-digital-minds-governance-prevent))_

Using the [Governance of Digital Minds](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1et-TIGBRbHg2lLBkKwCCQCrq2p975b8q1KdpP_nnnpI/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.cuighsf9mc3l) primer as inspiration, choose either: 
- one area of **recent legal action** _or_ 
- one **legal framework**
**Spend 10 minutes **noting down how it may or may not apply to digital minds, in the context of risks of over- and under-attribution of moral status. We will discuss your responses during the discussion session.

chunks.chunkContent:
**Welcome to Unit 8!**

This unit is your opportunity to consolidate what you’ve learnt on this course, and make a contribution to your group. Much of the material for this week is focussed in the **brainstorming doc in the written prompt**. 

We will cover:
- What are the main organisations involved in digital minds work, and how might you get involved?
- What are you taking away from this course? 
- What 4 minute contribution would you like to share with your group?

By the end of this Unit, you should be able to:
- Identify relevant organisations and institutions working in and around digital minds
- Examine current work and research on digital minds and identify gaps
- Analyse principles for research on digital minds
- Articulate your thinking around digital minds questions

**We hope you enjoy this Unit!** Please add any feedback inline, and reach out to online-course@digitalminds.cam with any questions.
